title: The bell-stand maker
hookLine: Woodworker Qing fasts until he forgets praise and reward, then carves (Zhuangzi 19)
last: FULLY PRESENT TO THE WEIGHT OF THE BUCKET.

cards: A wooden stand for hanging bells, finished and set out where people can see it. In the story, everyone who looks at it is startled. It seems too good for human hands, as if spirits made it.
The ruler of Lu sees it too, and he questions the woodworker, a man named Qing. What technique? What training?
What trick? Qing's answer, in the Chinese book called the Zhuangzi, isn't about chisels at all. It's about what he had to forget before he picked one up.
Today's word is the craftsman himself: Qing.

teach.b: First, the answer begins humbly. Qing says, in paraphrase, I'm only a workman, what art could I have? But there is one thing.
Before he makes a bell-stand, he fasts, to make his mind still. Second, what the fast takes away. After three days, the text says, he no longer thinks of congratulations, reward, rank or pay.
After five days, he no longer thinks of praise or blame, of being skillful or clumsy. After seven days, he forgets even his own limbs and body, and the ruler's court has dropped out of his mind.
Notice the order: first the paycheck, then the audience, then the self who wanted both. Third, what's left. Only then does Qing walk into the forest.
He looks at the trees, at their natural shape, until he finds one where he can already see the bell-stand inside it. Then he sets his hand to it.

teach.h: HE SEES IT IN THE TREE.
teach.b: If he can't see it, he leaves the tree alone. The Zhuangzi calls this, in paraphrase, heaven meeting heaven: what's natural in the worker meeting what's natural in the wood. Fourth, why this still speaks to a modern desk.
Work can come with a prize always in view: the likes, the raise. Qing's story doesn't say rewards are evil. It says they get in the way of seeing.
Work done while watching the audience is done half-looking.
The bell-stand that startled everyone came from someone who, for a while, had stopped caring whether it would.

how: Readers of the Zhuangzi, including Daoist teachers and students of Chinese philosophy, often turn to Qing's story when talking about craft, focus and working without attachment to reward.

o: the Zhuangzi's woodworker who fasted until reward fell away
a Confucian teacher who taught music with temple bells
a Chinese emperor who demanded perfect bell-stands

p: forgets his own limbs and body
sees the bell-stand in the tree

s: Qing tells the ruler his secret is a special chisel technique
his answer is about fasting to still the mind and forget reward and praise.
Qing only carves when he can see the bell-stand in the tree
if he can't see it, he leaves the tree alone.
in the story, the first thing he forgets is his body
reward and pay go first, then praise and blame, then his limbs and body.

games.q: you're Qing. the ruler of Lu demands the secret of your bell-stand. what do you tell him?
o: I studied with a great master.
I'm only a workman, but I fast to still my mind first.
it's a family secret I can't share.
games.why: he calls himself only a workman, then describes fasting until he forgets reward, praise and even his body.

practice: Hold a piece of work ahead of you today and, like Qing, set things down one at a time: first what you'll get for it, then what people will say about it, then even the worry about whether you're good enough.
What's left is the task itself and the material in front of you; rest there. If you pray, you can bring the work in your own tradition's words.

wordCard.voice: Qing. The woodworker in the Zhuangzi who fasted until he forgot reward and praise, then saw the bell-stand inside the tree. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: forget the prize. What's left is the work, and the wood. That's day nine hundred one.
